title: Heritage sites in Nagaland: Kohima, Dimapur ruins and Naga villages
seo_title: Heritage Sites in Nagaland: Kohima, Dimapur and Villages
meta_description: Heritage sites in Nagaland: Kohima War Cemetery, the Kachari ruins at Dimapur, Kisama heritage village, Khonoma and the State Museum, with tips for groups.
summary: Nagaland's heritage sits in three layers. The Kachari ruins at Dimapur, with their carved mushroom-shaped pillars, belong to a medieval Dimasa capital. Kohima War Cemetery marks the 1944 battle that stopped the Japanese advance into India. Naga villages such as Khonoma and the Kisama heritage village keep the architecture, crafts and customs of more than a dozen Naga peoples.

paras: Nagaland is home to many distinct Naga peoples, among them the Angami, Ao, Konyak, Sumi, Lotha, Chakhesang and Sangtam, each with its own language, dress, house forms and village organisation. Most of the state's heritage is living heritage: morungs (village dormitories), carved log drums, memorial stones, terraced fields and festivals tied to the farming year. Our page on [tribes of India](tribes-of-india.html) sets this in a national frame.

There is no UNESCO World Heritage Site in Nagaland. What the state offers instead is the chance to see how archaeology, oral history and colonial records each tell part of a story, and where they disagree.

In the middle of Dimapur town stands a group of tall carved stone pillars with rounded, mushroom-like tops, along with the remains of a brick gateway and enclosure. They are associated with the Dimasa Kachari kingdom, which had its capital here before Ahom attacks in the 16th century pushed the court south to Maibong. The site is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.

The pillars carry carved motifs of animals, plants and geometric designs, but their exact purpose is debated. Some scholars read them as memorials, others as markers linked to fertility or royal ritual. It is a good site for students to practise separating what the stones show from what is later claimed about them. Our lecture [Excavation headlines: evidence or exaggeration?](excavation-headlines-evidence-or-exaggeration.html) builds exactly that habit.

sections.h2: Kohima: the 1944 battle and its memory
paras: In April to June 1944, Kohima saw one of the hardest fought battles of the Second World War in Asia, as British and Indian troops halted the Japanese advance towards India. The Kohima War Cemetery, maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, is laid out on the slopes of Garrison Hill where much of the fighting took place, including the area around the Deputy Commissioner's tennis court.

The memorial to the 2nd British Division carries the well known epitaph beginning 'When you go home, tell them of us and say'. It is a place to discuss how war is remembered, whose names are carved and whose are missing, including the Naga villagers who carried supplies and guided troops. Our lecture on [cemeteries, epitaphs and public memory](cemeteries-epitaphs-and-public-memory.html) uses sites like this one.

sections.h2: Villages, morungs and the Hornbill Festival
paras: Khonoma, an Angami village near Kohima, is known for its terraced rice fields, stone gateways and its record of resistance to British forces in 1879 to 1880. It later became known for community conservation of its forests. Touphema, also near Kohima, runs a village tourism model with traditional houses. In Mon district, Konyak villages such as Longwa straddle the Myanmar border.

The Naga Heritage Village at Kisama, south of Kohima, has a morung for each major Naga people and hosts the Hornbill Festival in the first ten days of December. It is a showcase rather than a living village, but it lets a group compare house forms and carvings from across the state in one afternoon.

sections.h2: Planning a heritage visit to Nagaland
paras: Indian visitors need an Inner Line Permit, and rules for foreign visitors should be checked before travel. Dimapur has the railway station and airport, and Kohima is a few hours' drive uphill. October to May is the comfortable season.

faq.q: What are the Kachari ruins in Dimapur?
faq.a: They are carved stone pillars with rounded tops and the remains of a brick gateway, linked to the Dimasa Kachari kingdom that had its capital at Dimapur before the 16th century. Their exact purpose is debated, with memorial and ritual readings both proposed. The site is protected by the ASI.

faq.q: Why is Kohima War Cemetery important?
faq.a: It marks the battle of Kohima in 1944, when British and Indian troops halted the Japanese advance into India. The cemetery lies on Garrison Hill where the fighting took place, and its memorial epitaph is one of the best known war inscriptions in the world.

faq.q: Are there UNESCO World Heritage Sites in Nagaland?
faq.a: No. Nagaland has no UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its heritage is mainly in the Dimapur ruins, Second World War sites at Kohima and the living culture of Naga villages, morungs and festivals.

faq.q: When is the Hornbill Festival held?
faq.a: The Hornbill Festival is held at the Naga Heritage Village, Kisama, near Kohima, usually from 1 to 10 December. It brings together dance, music, crafts and food from across the Naga peoples. Book transport and stays well ahead.
